title: Temporal Abstraction and Option Keyboard
abstract:
We discuss temporal abstraction and the Option Keyboard, where instead of operating only at the level of primitive actions, RL agents could reason over temporally extended “options” or “skills.” This kind of abstraction has been shown to help with exploration and credit assignment, and makes behaviors reusable across tasks. Our plan would be to cover the core ideas behind the options framework, then dive into the Option Keyboard, which uses successor features and generalized policy improvement to combine existing skills on the fly, letting an agent tackle new tasks without retraining from scratch.

Additional Details:
Under the options framework, an RL agent can reason about and take a sequence of actions at each decision point. This is in contrast to the standard RL setting, where the agent only reasons about and takes a single action at each timestep. The central hope behind using options is the fact that for many long-horizon, real-world tasks, useful behavior often involves chaining together skills like “walk to the door” or “pick up the key.” Think about getting to the airport: we don’t plan every muscle twitch along the way. Instead, we reason at coarser time scales, such as walking to the bus stop, riding to the airport, and heading to check-in. (Many real-world tasks can be decomposed like this across multiple time scales.) The options framework formalizes these chunks using options. Each option is a temporally extended behavior defined by an initiation set, an internal policy, and a termination condition. Planning and learning over options rather than primitive actions can speed up exploration, improve credit assignment, and make skills reusable across tasks.

The Option Keyboard asks a natural follow-up question: once an agent has a set of skills, can it combine them to produce new behaviors without learning from scratch? Using successor features and generalized policy improvement (GPI), the Option Keyboard lets an agent express a new task as a weighted combination of the objectives underlying its existing options. Much like pressing several keys at once to play a chord, the agent can “play” combinations of basic skills to generate a much richer repertoire of behaviors (hence the name "keyboard"!).

title: Long-term and Short-term Memory in RL Agents
abstract:
We discuss how an RL agent should manage its memory when operating in a continual RL setting. (By memory, we essentially mean the collection of various objects that an agent might maintain; see below for details.) For instance, one way of dealing with memory in continual RL is to maintain long-term and short-term memory components, e.g.
- (long-term memory:) replay buffers, environment models, slowly changing network weights (e.g. permanent networks in some continual RL work)
- (short-term memory:) an RNN's hidden state, recent history of the agent, fast changing network weights (e.g. transient networks in some continual RL work)

Additional Details:
RL agents need to store various objects while trying to learn a desirable behavior in their environment. Almost always, this will include storing the agent's policy, say, in the form of network weights. Based on the learning algorithm being used, the agent could also store estimates of value functions and environment models, maintain replay buffers, etc. And once the agent identifies a desirable behavior, it need not change the various objects it stored earlier. This is what happens in the setting of classical RL. However, this changes in the setting of continual RL.

The setting of continual RL considers some interesting modifications to the classical RL setting, such as introducing partial-observability and non-stationarity in the MDP's transition dynamics, or constraining the agent's memory and compute relative to the "size" of the MDP. In contrast to the situation in classical RL, in continual RL, it seems that the agent's estimates of the various objects, such as value functions, necessarily need to be transient, i.e. they need to be regularly updated with the agent's experience, either because the underlying system keeps changing or because the agent can only maintain local approximations of the relevant objects with high-enough fidelity due to its constrained form.
